strengths: Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 5 Overcooked layouts with well-chosen baselines (BC, MEP, HSP, HSP-ft, HSP-meta) and human study with 36 participants providing real-world validation
Demonstrated rapid in-context adaptation within 5-8 episodes with convincing learning curves (Figure 3) and robustness to non-stationary partners (average 3.67 episodes to adapt)

Consistent improvements especially pronounced on complex coordination tasks (Multi-recipe: 28.28 reward/0.30 BR-prox vs HSP 21.37/0.23), with strong human evaluation results (COOT 63.5 vs baselines 40.5-53.0)
Solid reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, algorithms, hardware specifications, and commitment to code release; thorough ablation studies justify design choices
Clear problem formulation addressing important multi-agent challenge; well-motivated and generally well-written with good use of figures and comprehensive appendix
weaknesses: Limited scope: Evaluation restricted to single environment (Overcooked); generalizability to other coordination domains undemonstrated. Claims require validation beyond structured grid-world setting

Training-test distribution mismatch: All 'unseen' test partners drawn from same HU-MG distribution with event-based rewards as training. True out-of-distribution robustness (different reward structures, behavioral paradigms) not evaluated—'unseen' means unseen identities within same family

Incremental technical novelty: Core contribution is applying existing Decision Transformer methods to coordination with standard GPT-2 and straightforward supervised training. Limited algorithmic innovation; deeper mechanistic understanding of how transformer learns partner preferences from trajectories lacking

Insufficient baseline analysis: HSP-meta failure (0.03 BR-prox Multi-recipe) attributed vaguely to 'reconstruction loss misalignment' without mechanistic explanation or ablations on encoder design. HSP-ft instability (Table 11) lacks analysis—unclear if failure inherent to fine-tuning in coordination or tuning issue. Dense-reward advantage for baselines mentioned but not resolved

Unexamined assumptions: Cross-entropy loss objective not justified—predicting isolated best-response actions insufficient for true coordination where partner's future actions depend on ego agent's past. Sensitivity to best-response policy quality unexplored. Human study limited to single layout with high variance

Methodological concerns: Best-response policies required for training create computational overhead (300 GPU hours, 36 agent pairs). Fixed 5-episode context window scalability to longer horizons unclear. Human study outlier exclusion (top/bottom 10%) could bias results

strengths: Comprehensive evaluation within scope: multiple baselines, ablations, and human study with 36 participants demonstrating clear preference for COOT
Valuable human evaluation showing COOT is preferred by human partners and adapts better than baselines in realistic human-AI collaboration
Clear and reproducible work with detailed hyperparameters, hardware specifications, and promised code release enabling reproduction
Well-motivated problem addressing the important challenge of adapting to unseen partners without parameter updates
weaknesses: Limited novelty: primarily applies existing Decision-Pretrained Transformers to coordination by training on best-response policies without introducing fundamentally new concepts or insights

Critical generalization concern: evaluation partners are NOT truly out-of-distribution—all use the same event-based hidden-reward framework as training partners, making this train-test distribution matching rather than genuine generalization to unseen behavior types

Narrow evaluation scope: only tested in Overcooked (single deterministic grid-world environment); human evaluation covers only one layout; no evaluation on qualitatively different partner types (imitation-learned, human-like, adversarial, stochastic)

Insufficient baseline comparisons: HSP-meta and HSP-ft underperformance may reflect poor tuning rather than fundamental limitations; PECAN (Lou et al. 2023)—a directly relevant baseline for behavior-conditioned coordination—is not empirically compared

Black-box mechanism without mechanistic insight: no explanation of how transformer uses context, what representations it learns, or why learning best-responses to known-reward partners transfers to unknown partners; no visualizations of attention or learned features

Lack of theoretical justification: no formal analysis of when/why best-response training transfers to unknown partners, no sample complexity analysis, and the event-based hidden-reward model is presented as natural but not rigorously justified

strengths: Well-motivated problem formulation addressing a gap between task-focused ICL and partner-behavior adaptation; clearly identifies why fine-tuning and Meta-RL fail for coordination
Comprehensive experimental validation including human study (36 participants) with both quantitative results and qualitative feedback—valuable validation often missing in multi-agent papers
Consistently strong empirical results across diverse Overcooked layouts, with particularly clear advantages in coordination-heavy environments (Multi-recipe: 28.28 vs HSP 21.37)
Methodologically sound with rigorous dataset construction (behavior-preferring agents, diversity sampling, train/eval separation) grounded in ZSC-eval framework
Excellent reproducibility: extensive implementation details, hyperparameters, hardware specs, promised code release, and honest limitation discussion
Good empirical insights such as demonstrating that temporal structure preservation (chunk-wise vs step-wise shuffling) matters for coordination, explaining why DPT augmentations don't transfer
Clear presentation with well-designed figures and logical flow; practical online deployment approach with FIFO context buffers
weaknesses: Severely limited environmental scope: evaluation restricted to Overcooked only (albeit 5 layouts). Generalization to continuous control, robotics, other game types, or real-world scenarios is completely unexplored, undermining broad applicability claims

Incremental technical contribution: straightforward application of Decision Pretrained Transformers (Lee et al. 2023) to coordination. Hidden-Utility Markov Game framework builds directly on ZSC-eval (Wang et al. 2024). No novel architectures, training procedures, or theoretical insights

Limited theoretical understanding of why in-context adaptation outperforms fine-tuning. No formal analysis of success conditions, mechanism interpretability (e.g., attention visualization), or theoretical guarantees

Baseline implementation concerns: HSP-meta dramatically underperforms vanilla HSP (20.44 vs 54.99 rewards in Bothway Coord.). Explanation provided but raises questions about fair implementation and tuning. Missing comparison to simpler context-conditioning baselines (e.g., BC with concatenated history)

Dataset construction and generalization limitations: training uses 36 agent pairs with specific hidden-utility structure. Sensitivity to number/composition of partners unexplored. Hidden-utility model may not capture realistic partner behaviors (human bounded rationality, learning, deception)
Computational efficiency gap: COOT inference 4.5× slower than BC (2.41 vs 0.54 ms per step). Inference requires processing full context histories; scalability and scaling behavior not analyzed

Human study limitations: tested on only one layout (Coord. Ring), no forced mid-task strategy changes, modest sample size (36), outlier removal could bias results. Would benefit from multiple layouts matching agent-based evaluation breadth

Missing technical details and ablations: query state construction details ('short history')—sensitivity unclear; no ablation on training partner count/composition; model architecture choice (GPT-2) not justified
Experimental variance: evaluation over only 50 rollouts with action sampling, large standard deviations sometimes (e.g., HSP-ft 41.30±9.85), no statistical significance testing between methods

Adaptation analysis could be deeper: partner-swap experiments use discrete switches rather than continuous drift or adversarial scenarios. Is 6-episode adaptation truly 'rapid' without domain-specific context?

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical coordination with unseen partners without expensive fine-tuning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks (Overcooked 5 layouts + GRF) with extensive baselines (HSP, MEP, PACE, HSP-meta, BC, fine-tuning)
Strong empirical results with consistent improvements in coordination-heavy layouts and clear few-shot adaptation advantage (Figure 2)
Valuable human study with 36 participants validating that COOT is perceived as more adaptive and preferred by 50% of participants
Thorough ablations examining context length, data augmentation strategies, and scaling properties
Excellent reproducibility with detailed hyperparameters, algorithms, hardware specs, and honest limitations discussion
Clever reframing of partner behavior generalization as in-context learning task adaptation
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core architecture is GPT-2 from prior work (DPT); training objective is standard supervised learning; contribution is primarily application rather than methodological innovation

Overstated generalization claims: all evaluation partners drawn from same training procedure (HSP/MEP behavior-preferring agents); no evaluation on truly novel behaviors or out-of-distribution partner types; Figure 6 shows poor cross-partner generalization

Concerning baseline performance: HSP-meta and PACE substantially underperform vanilla HSP across most layouts (Table 1), contradicting their intended advantages; tuned HSP-meta degrades on most layouts (Table 8); raises fairness/implementation concerns
Missing comparison with concurrent work (TAGET, Zhang et al. 2025), a recent transformer-based baseline for ad-hoc teamwork

Fundamental context length limitation: performance degrades significantly with contexts >5 episodes (Table 15); context masking doesn't solve this; suggests model may not learn robust long-term partner representations

Heavy dependence on training diversity: requires 36 training partners; performance drops 24% reducing to 12 partners (Table 18); scalability of generating diverse training populations in new domains unclear; data generation cost (315K examples) is substantial

Limited multi-agent scalability: GRF uses only 3 agents total with modest improvements (2.50 vs 1.46 goal rate); no evaluation beyond 3-agent teams; unclear how method scales to realistic multi-agent systems

Critical analysis gaps: no ablation on best-response learning necessity; no failure case analysis; no representation analysis (attention visualizations, embedding studies); no investigation of why baselines fail so dramatically
Human study limited to single layout (Coord. Ring) with 36 participants; limited analysis of why COOT is preferred; no comparison with true best-response policies
Artificial evaluation protocol: strict no-prior protocol unrealistic; real coordination often has prior interaction history; acknowledged possibility of context pre-filling not explored

strengths: Addresses important problem of efficient multi-agent coordination without fine-tuning
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple environments, baselines, and ablations
Human study (36 participants) validates human perception of adaptivity and collaboration quality
Honest acknowledgment of limitations and extensive implementation details in appendices
Consistent improvements in coordination-heavy layouts with detailed analysis of adaptation dynamics
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: primarily applies existing GPT-2 architecture to reformulated problem with supervised learning objective
Unfair experimental comparisons: COOT uses sparse rewards while HSP/MEP use dense reward shaping (acknowledged in Table 26 but not controlled in main results)
Baseline implementation concerns: HSP-meta dramatically underperforms vanilla HSP (29.84 vs 41.10 on Coord. Ring), suggesting potential fairness issues
Modest practical improvements: 16% relative BR-prox gain over HSP with high baseline uncertainty; minimal advantage in simple layouts
Critical cold-start limitation: strict no-prior protocol leaves COOT at 0.19 BR-prox in episode 1, severely limiting real-world deployment
Context window degradation: performance drops beyond 5 episodes (41.11→36.04), suggesting pattern-matching rather than robust partner modeling
Limited generalization evidence: all evaluation partners are same-algorithm family (HSP/MEP with event-based rewards); no evaluation on fundamentally different training paradigms
Insufficient mechanistic understanding: no analysis of what transformer learns; no interpretation of attention or context components; posterior sampling claims unvalidated
Missing ablation on data requirements: 36 best-response policies with 250 trajectories each represents substantial overhead not adequately discussed
Human study tested only one layout (Coord. Ring) with 36 participants; qualitative LLM analysis lacks validation

strengths: Novel problem framing: Elegant reframing of partner adaptation as an in-context learning problem distinct from task-focused ICL, with clear motivation for avoiding latent representation bottlenecks
Comprehensive experimental validation: Multiple environments (5+ Overcooked layouts, GRF), diverse baselines (8+ methods), 36-participant human studies, careful ablations on all design choices

Strong and consistent empirical results: Pronounced improvements on coordination-heavy layouts (45.96 vs 29.35 for Coord. Ring Multi-recipe), rapid few-shot adaptation within 5-15 episodes, human preferences align with quantitative metrics
Excellent reproducibility: Detailed hyperparameters, computational specifications, training times, complete algorithms, thorough appendices enabling reproduction
Rigorous investigation of baseline underperformance: Systematic hyperparameter search for HSP-meta (7 configurations), hypotheses for why latent encodings fail, additional comparisons in appendices
Robust and practical advantages: No parameter updates at test-time, works with sparse rewards, adapts to non-stationary partners within ~6 episodes, validated in human studies
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: Uses standard GPT-2 architecture from existing DPT work; dataset generation largely adapted from HSP; core contribution is novel application rather than fundamental technical innovation

Scalability concerns inadequately addressed: Largest team tested is 3 agents; no analysis of transformer inference cost scaling with context; unclear performance on continuous control or high-dimensional observations; context degradation at 7+ episodes suggests fundamental limits

Expensive training setup with limited analysis: Requires training 36+ behavioral agents + best-response pairs (~19 hrs per layout); Table 18 shows graceful degradation but limited scope (24% drop); unclear minimum partner diversity for new domains

Surprising baseline underperformance warrants deeper investigation: HSP-meta and PACE substantially underperform vanilla HSP; while Appendix B.3 explores hyperparameters, core hypotheses about encoder reconstruction loss lack rigorous validation; equal tuning effort unclear

Training-evaluation population overlap: Both populations from same HSP pool; behavioral divergence (JS 0.33 vs 0.30 for random) is modest; true out-of-distribution generalization unclear despite DPP-based selection

Context design limitations: Fixed 5-episode context appears somewhat arbitrary; outdated information at 7+ episodes unresolved; proposed improvements (attention-based recency, hierarchical selection) left for future work; step-wise shuffling hurting performance suggests brittle temporal structure

Missing failure case analysis: No systematic exploration of when COOT fails; counter-intuitive performance variation across partners unexplained; intra-episode compounding errors acknowledged but not quantified

Insufficient architectural analysis: No ablation on transformer choices (depth, width, attention heads); no visualization of learned partner behavior representations; sensitivity to event-based diversity score unexplored
